en.title: Medicine (MBBS): the whole course
en.short: How a medical degree is organised, from basic sciences to clinical care, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What medicine is
sections.text:
Medicine is the science and practice of preventing, diagnosing and treating disease. It joins biological knowledge with communication, judgement and ethics. A doctor must understand how the body works, how it fails, and how to help a particular person in a particular setting.

These summaries teach concepts to students. They are not medical advice and do not replace teachers, textbooks or official guidelines. They do not give drug doses. Guidelines change, and they differ between countries, so always check the current national or World Health Organization (WHO) source. Anyone who is unwell or in crisis should seek local medical help.

sections.heading: How the degree is organised
sections.text:
The degree has several names, including MBBS and MBChB. It usually lasts five or six years, and some countries also offer a graduate entry route. Many programmes begin with a premedical year of chemistry, physics and biology. Preclinical years follow, then clinical years in hospitals and communities.

After graduation, doctors complete a supervised period before full registration. It is called housemanship in Nigeria and Ghana, internship in Kenya and South Africa, and the Foundation Programme in the UK. Medical councils set these rules, and each country has its own. Some schools teach in integrated organ-system blocks instead of separate subjects, but the content is much the same.

sections.heading: The basic sciences
sections.text:
Teaching normally starts with the normal body. Anatomy describes structure, and histology and embryology add its microscopic form and its development. Physiology explains function. Biochemistry and genetics explain the molecules behind both. Immunology explains how the body defends itself.

The next stage explains disease and its treatment. Pathology studies how disease changes cells and organs. Microbiology studies the organisms that cause infection. Pharmacology studies how medicines act and how the body handles them. These subjects form the link between the laboratory and the patient.

sections.heading: The clinical years
sections.text:
Students learn history taking and physical examination first, because they lead to most diagnoses. They then rotate through the main clinical areas: internal medicine, surgery, paediatrics, obstetrics and gynaecology, psychiatry, and community health.

Common conditions receive special weight. In many African countries these include malaria, HIV, tuberculosis and sickle cell disease. Hypertension and diabetes are rising everywhere. Ethics and professionalism run through every year.

At master’s level, and in research projects, students study epidemiology, evidence-based medicine and research methods. These skills help a doctor judge new evidence throughout a career.

sections.heading: How to study medicine
sections.text:
The volume of content is large, so understanding must come before memorising. Link each disease to the normal structure and function that it disturbs. For example, connect sickle cell pain to a change in one amino acid, then to haemoglobin polymers, and then to blocked small vessels.

Test yourself often instead of only rereading. Space your revision over weeks. Draw pathways and anatomy from memory. Practise with past questions, including single best answer questions and the objective structured clinical examination (OSCE), which tests practical skills at timed stations.

See real patients early, with permission and supervision. A patient’s story makes facts easier to remember. Look after your own sleep and mental health as well. Medical school is demanding, and asking for help from a tutor, counsellor or doctor is sensible.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often learn lists of symptoms without the mechanism, and then cannot reason through an unfamiliar case. Others jump to a diagnosis and stop looking, which is called premature closure. Some order many tests without first asking what each result would change.

In examinations, candidates often forget to mention safety and urgent actions first, or they ignore the setting and available resources. They may also quote one country’s guideline as if it were universal.

Another serious mistake is to treat oneself, relatives or friends from notes such as these. Clinical decisions need a qualified clinician who can assess the person directly.

keyPoints: Medicine moves from normal structure and function to disease, treatment and clinical care.
Clinical years cover medicine, surgery, paediatrics, obstetrics and gynaecology, psychiatry and community health.
History taking and examination lead to most diagnoses.
Understand mechanisms first, then test yourself often.
Guidelines change and differ between countries, so check the current official source.
These summaries teach concepts and are not medical advice.

en.title: Anatomy: language, limbs and nerves
en.short: The terms of anatomy, the musculoskeletal system, peripheral nerves and why they matter clinically.

sections.heading: The language of anatomy
sections.text:
Anatomy describes the body from a fixed reference called the anatomical position. The person stands upright and faces forward, with arms by the sides and palms facing forward. All directions refer to this position, whichever way the patient is lying.

Three planes divide the body. A sagittal plane separates left and right. A coronal plane separates front and back. A transverse plane separates upper and lower parts. Medial means nearer the midline, and lateral means further from it. Proximal means nearer the attachment of a limb, and distal means further from it. Exact terms prevent errors. A surgeon must know precisely which structure a colleague means.

sections.heading: Bones, joints and muscles
sections.text: The adult skeleton has about 206 bones. Joints are fibrous, cartilaginous or synovial. Synovial joints, such as the knee, have a capsule and lubricating fluid, and they allow the most movement. Muscles usually cross a joint and move the bone on which they insert. A useful habit is to learn each muscle with its nerve supply and action, because this explains the signs of injury.

sections.heading: Nerves and clinical anatomy
sections.text:
There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves. A dermatome is the skin area supplied by one spinal nerve root. For example, T4 supplies skin near the nipple and T10 supplies skin near the umbilicus. A myotome is the group of muscles supplied by one root.

The brachial plexus, usually formed from roots C5 to T1, supplies the upper limb. Knowing nerve paths predicts injuries:
Radial nerve injury in a fracture of the humeral shaft can cause wrist drop.
Median nerve compression at the wrist causes carpal tunnel syndrome.
Common fibular nerve injury at the neck of the fibula can cause foot drop.

These patterns show why anatomy remains useful at the bedside. They also guide safe injection sites and surgical incisions.

keyPoints: All anatomical terms refer to the anatomical position.
Sagittal, coronal and transverse are the three main planes.
Synovial joints allow the most movement.
A dermatome is the skin supplied by one spinal nerve root.
The brachial plexus usually arises from C5 to T1.
Learn each muscle with its nerve and action.

en.title: Anatomy of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis
en.short: Heart, lungs, gut blood supply, the portal system and pelvic relations, with clinical examples.

sections.heading: The thorax
sections.text:
The thorax contains the lungs and the mediastinum, which is the central space holding the heart, great vessels, trachea and oesophagus. The right lung has three lobes and the left lung has two. The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical, so inhaled objects often enter it.

Blood reaches the right atrium and passes to the right ventricle, then to the lungs. It returns to the left atrium, passes to the left ventricle, and leaves through the aorta. The right and left coronary arteries supply the heart muscle. The phrenic nerve, from roots C3 to C5, supplies the diaphragm. This explains why a high neck injury can stop breathing.

sections.heading: The abdomen
sections.text:
The abdomen is described in four quadrants or nine regions. The peritoneum is a thin membrane that lines the abdominal wall and covers many organs. The kidneys lie behind it, so they are called retroperitoneal.

The gut has three blood supplies. The coeliac trunk supplies the foregut, the superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut, and the inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut. The portal vein carries blood from the gut and spleen to the liver. When the liver is scarred, as in chronic hepatitis B, or when portal flow is blocked, as in chronic schistosomiasis, portal pressure rises. Veins at the lower oesophagus can then enlarge into varices, which may bleed severely.

sections.heading: The pelvis and referred pain
sections.text:
The pelvis holds the bladder, rectum and reproductive organs. In women, the ureter passes beneath the uterine artery near the cervix. It can therefore be injured during a hysterectomy.

Internal organs are poorly localised by sensory nerves, so pain can be felt away from its source. Early appendicitis often causes central abdominal pain around the T10 dermatome. Pain moves to the right iliac fossa once the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed.

keyPoints: The right lung has three lobes and the left has two.
The phrenic nerve comes from C3 to C5.
Coeliac trunk, superior and inferior mesenteric arteries supply the fore, mid and hind gut.
Portal hypertension can cause bleeding oesophageal varices.
The ureter runs beneath the uterine artery.
Visceral pain is often felt away from its source.

en.title: Cells, histology and embryology
en.short: Cell structure, the four basic tissues, cell division and how the embryo develops.

sections.heading: The cell
sections.text:
The cell is the basic unit of life. Its plasma membrane is a lipid bilayer containing proteins that control what enters and leaves. The nucleus stores DNA. Mitochondria produce most of the cell’s ATP. Ribosomes make proteins, and the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus process and package them. Lysosomes break down waste.

Mitosis produces two genetically identical cells for growth and repair. Meiosis produces gametes with half the normal chromosome number. Errors in chromosome separation during meiosis can cause conditions such as trisomy 21, also called Down syndrome.

sections.heading: The four basic tissues
sections.text:
Histology is the microscopic study of tissues. All organs are built from four tissue types:
Epithelium covers surfaces and lines tubes. It is classified by cell shape and number of layers.
Connective tissue supports and binds. It includes bone, cartilage, fat and blood.
Muscle tissue contracts. It can be skeletal, cardiac or smooth.
Nervous tissue carries and processes signals.

Histology prepares students for pathology, because many diseases are diagnosed by comparing an abnormal tissue sample with normal structure.

sections.heading: Early development
sections.text:
Fertilisation forms a zygote, which divides as it travels to the uterus. Implantation occurs about one week after fertilisation. In the third week, gastrulation creates three germ layers:
Ectoderm forms the skin and nervous system.
Mesoderm forms muscle, bone, the heart and most of the urogenital system.
Endoderm forms the lining of the gut and airways.

The neural tube closes during the fourth week, often before a woman knows she is pregnant. Failure can cause spina bifida or anencephaly. Adequate folate before conception reduces this risk, which is why public health programmes promote folic acid.

The main organs form from about week 3 to week 8. The embryo is then most sensitive to teratogens, which are agents that cause birth defects. Examples are rubella virus, alcohol and thalidomide.

keyPoints: Mitosis gives identical cells, and meiosis gives gametes.
The four basic tissues are epithelium, connective tissue, muscle and nerve.
Gastrulation forms ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm in week 3.
The neural tube closes during week 4.
Folate before conception reduces neural tube defects.
Teratogens do most harm during organ formation.

en.title: Physiology of the heart and lungs
en.short: Homeostasis, cardiac output, blood pressure, gas exchange and the control of breathing.

sections.heading: Homeostasis
sections.text: Physiology explains how the healthy body works. Its central idea is homeostasis, the maintenance of a stable internal environment. Most control systems use negative feedback, in which a change triggers a response that reverses it. Failure of a control system often produces disease.

sections.heading: The circulation
sections.text:
Cardiac output is the volume of blood the heart pumps each minute. It equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume.
Worked example: 70 beats per minute × 70 mL per beat = 4,900 mL per minute, or about 4.9 L per minute.

The Frank-Starling mechanism states that more filling stretches heart muscle and produces a stronger contraction, up to a limit. Mean arterial pressure equals cardiac output multiplied by total peripheral resistance. Small arterioles provide most of this resistance.

Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch detect pressure. If pressure falls, sympathetic activity rises and parasympathetic activity falls. Heart rate and vessel tone then increase. Over longer periods, the kidneys control pressure by adjusting blood volume.

sections.heading: Breathing and gas exchange
sections.text:
Ventilation moves air, and diffusion moves gases across the thin wall of the alveoli. Good gas exchange needs air and blood to match, which is called ventilation-perfusion matching. Mismatch is the most common cause of low oxygen in lung disease.

Most oxygen travels bound to haemoglobin. The oxygen dissociation curve is S-shaped, because binding of one oxygen molecule makes the next one bind more easily. The curve shifts to the right with raised CO₂, acidity, temperature or 2,3-BPG. Haemoglobin then releases oxygen more easily to active tissues.

The main stimulus to breathe is CO₂, detected through pH changes by central chemoreceptors in the medulla. Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies respond mainly to low oxygen. A resting adult normally takes about 12 to 20 breaths each minute.

keyPoints: Homeostasis mostly relies on negative feedback.
Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume.
Mean arterial pressure = cardiac output × peripheral resistance.
Baroreceptors give fast control, and the kidneys give long-term control of pressure.
A right shift of the oxygen curve releases oxygen to tissues.
CO₂ is the main normal stimulus to breathe.

en.title: Kidneys, body fluids and acid-base balance
en.short: The nephron, fluid compartments, the hormones of fluid balance and how to read acid-base results.

sections.heading: Body fluids
sections.text:
Water makes up about 60% of body weight in a typical young adult man, and less in women and older people. About two-thirds lies inside cells, and one-third lies outside them.
Worked example: A 70 kg man has about 42 L of water (70 × 0.6). About 28 L is intracellular and 14 L is extracellular.

This matters in clinical practice. Fluid lost in severe diarrhoea comes first from the extracellular space, including the blood volume. In cholera, this can quickly cause shock.

sections.heading: The nephron
sections.text:
Each kidney contains about one million nephrons. Blood is filtered at the glomerulus, and the tubule then reabsorbs most of the filtrate and secretes some substances. The normal glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is about 90 to 120 mL per minute in healthy adults, and it falls with age and kidney disease.

Two hormone systems are central. When renal blood flow falls, renin leads to angiotensin II, which constricts vessels, and aldosterone, which retains sodium and water. Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct when the blood becomes too concentrated. Many blood pressure medicines act on these systems.

sections.heading: Acid-base balance
sections.text:
Normal arterial pH is about 7.35 to 7.45. The bicarbonate buffer links CO₂ and bicarbonate. The lungs control CO₂ within minutes, and the kidneys control bicarbonate over days.

To read a blood gas, first check the pH. Next, ask whether CO₂ or bicarbonate explains it. Then look for compensation.

In metabolic acidosis, the anion gap helps to find the cause. Anion gap = sodium − (chloride + bicarbonate).
Worked example: Sodium 140, chloride 100 and bicarbonate 12 mmol/L give a gap of 28 mmol/L, which is high. A raised gap suggests added acid, as in diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis or some poisonings. Normal ranges vary between laboratories.

keyPoints: Body water is about 60% of weight in a young man.
Two-thirds of water is intracellular.
Renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone retain sodium and raise pressure.
ADH increases water reabsorption.
Lungs adjust CO₂ fast, and kidneys adjust bicarbonate slowly.
Anion gap = sodium − (chloride + bicarbonate).

en.title: Nerve, muscle and endocrine physiology
en.short: Action potentials, synapses, the autonomic system, muscle contraction and hormone control.

sections.heading: Nerve signals
sections.text:
A neurone at rest has a negative charge inside, mainly because of potassium movement and the sodium-potassium pump. When a stimulus reaches threshold, sodium channels open and sodium rushes in. This is depolarisation. Potassium then leaves, which restores the charge. The wave of change is the action potential. Myelin speeds its travel.

At a synapse, the signal releases a neurotransmitter that binds to receptors on the next cell. Many medicines act here. For that reason, knowing receptors helps with the later study of pharmacology.

sections.heading: The autonomic system and muscle
sections.text:
The autonomic nervous system controls involuntary functions. The sympathetic division prepares the body for stress. It raises heart rate and widens the pupils and the airways. The parasympathetic division supports rest and digestion. It acts largely through the vagus nerve and uses acetylcholine.

At the neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine triggers an action potential in the muscle. Calcium is then released inside the fibre and binds to troponin, which exposes sites on actin. Myosin heads bind to actin and pull, using ATP. Myasthenia gravis, in which antibodies attack acetylcholine receptors, shows what follows when this step fails.

sections.heading: Hormones
sections.text:
Hormones are chemical messengers carried in the blood. The hypothalamus controls the anterior pituitary, which in turn controls the thyroid, adrenal cortex and gonads. Each axis uses negative feedback.

The thyroid axis is a clear example. TRH from the hypothalamus stimulates TSH from the pituitary, and TSH stimulates thyroid hormone. Rising thyroid hormone then suppresses TRH and TSH. In primary hypothyroidism, thyroid hormone is low and TSH is high. Iodine deficiency remains a cause of goitre in some regions.

The pancreas also controls blood glucose. Insulin lowers it by moving glucose into cells and promoting storage. Glucagon raises it by releasing stored glucose. Cortisol and adrenaline also raise glucose during stress.

keyPoints: Sodium entry causes depolarisation, and potassium exit restores the charge.
Myelin speeds nerve conduction.
Sympathetic means stress response; parasympathetic means rest and digestion.
Calcium binding to troponin allows muscle contraction.
Hormone axes use negative feedback.
Primary hypothyroidism shows low thyroid hormone and high TSH.

en.title: Biochemistry and metabolism
en.short: Enzymes, energy pathways, fat and protein metabolism, vitamins and common clinical links.

sections.heading: Enzymes
sections.text: Enzymes are biological catalysts. They speed reactions without being used up, and most are proteins. The Michaelis constant, Km, is the substrate concentration at half the maximum rate. A competitive inhibitor binds to the active site and raises the apparent Km. A non-competitive inhibitor lowers the maximum rate. Many medicines work by inhibiting enzymes. Statins, for example, inhibit HMG-CoA reductase in cholesterol synthesis.

sections.heading: Producing energy
sections.text:
Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm and breaks glucose into two pyruvate molecules, with a net gain of two ATP. When oxygen is present, pyruvate enters the mitochondria and joins the Krebs cycle. Oxidative phosphorylation then produces most of the ATP. One glucose molecule yields about 30 ATP in total.

Without enough oxygen, pyruvate becomes lactate. This explains the raised lactate in severe shock and severe malaria.

In fasting, the liver releases glucose from glycogen and then makes new glucose by gluconeogenesis. Fatty acids are burned and form ketone bodies, which the brain can use. When insulin is absent, as in untreated type 1 diabetes, ketone production can become dangerous and cause ketoacidosis.

sections.heading: Nutrition and clinical links
sections.text:
Biochemistry explains many deficiency diseases:
Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, because collagen synthesis fails.
Thiamine deficiency causes beriberi and Wernicke encephalopathy, because energy pathways need it.
Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency cause macrocytic anaemia, because DNA synthesis slows.
Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets in children.

Severe protein-energy malnutrition presents as marasmus, with severe wasting, or kwashiorkor, with oedema.

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is an X-linked condition common in malaria regions. Red cells cannot make enough NADPH to protect themselves from oxidation. Some antimalarial medicines, some other drugs and fava beans can then cause haemolysis. This is why testing matters before certain medicines are prescribed.

keyPoints: Enzymes are catalysts and common drug targets.
Glycolysis gives a net two ATP; oxidative phosphorylation gives most ATP.
Low oxygen shifts pyruvate to lactate.
Without insulin, ketone production can cause ketoacidosis.
G6PD deficiency is X-linked and can cause drug-triggered haemolysis.
Marasmus is wasting; kwashiorkor includes oedema.

en.title: Molecular biology and genetics
en.short: From DNA to protein, types of mutation, patterns of inheritance and genetic counselling.

sections.heading: From gene to protein
sections.text:
DNA stores information in a code of four bases. A gene is transcribed into messenger RNA in the nucleus, and ribosomes translate this RNA into a chain of amino acids. Three bases, called a codon, specify each amino acid.

A mutation is a change in DNA. A point mutation changes one base. A frameshift mutation adds or removes a number of bases that is not a multiple of three, which alters the reading of everything after it. Sickle cell disease is a classic point mutation. In the beta-globin gene, one base change replaces glutamic acid with valine at position 6 of the protein.

sections.heading: Patterns of inheritance
sections.text:
Single-gene conditions follow predictable patterns:
Autosomal dominant: one altered copy is enough, as in Marfan syndrome and Huntington disease.
Autosomal recessive: two altered copies are needed, as in sickle cell disease and cystic fibrosis.
X-linked recessive: mostly affects males, as in haemophilia A and G6PD deficiency.

Worked example: Two parents who both carry the sickle gene (AS) have four possible combinations in each pregnancy: AA, AS, SA and SS. Each pregnancy has a 1 in 4 chance of SS, a 1 in 2 chance of AS, and a 1 in 4 chance of AA. These chances apply to every pregnancy separately. Having one affected child does not change the chance for the next.

Many common conditions, including hypertension and type 2 diabetes, are multifactorial. They arise from many genes acting with the environment.

sections.heading: Tools and counselling
sections.text:
The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) copies small pieces of DNA, and it is widely used to diagnose infections and mutations. Sequencing reads the exact order of bases.

Genetic counselling gives people accurate information in a supportive way so that they can make their own decisions. A counsellor does not tell people what to choose and avoids blame. Results can affect relatives, so confidentiality needs special care. Local laws and services differ between countries.

keyPoints: DNA is transcribed into RNA and translated into protein.
A codon has three bases.
Sickle cell disease comes from a single base change in the beta-globin gene.
Two AS parents have a 1 in 4 chance of SS in each pregnancy.
Genetic counselling supports choice and does not direct it.
Common diseases are usually multifactorial.

en.title: Immunology
en.short: Innate and adaptive immunity, antibodies, vaccines, hypersensitivity and immune failure.

sections.heading: Two arms of immunity
sections.text:
Innate immunity responds quickly and in the same way each time. It includes skin, mucous membranes, complement proteins, neutrophils, macrophages and natural killer cells. These cells recognise common microbial patterns.

Adaptive immunity is slower, highly specific and has memory. B cells make antibodies. Helper T cells, which carry the CD4 molecule, coordinate the response. Cytotoxic T cells, which carry CD8, kill infected cells. T cells recognise antigens on MHC molecules, also called HLA in humans. HIV damages the immune system by infecting CD4 cells.

sections.heading: Antibodies and vaccines
sections.text:
There are five antibody classes. IgM appears first in an infection. IgG is the main long-term antibody and crosses the placenta, which protects newborn babies. IgA protects mucous surfaces and is present in breast milk. IgE takes part in allergy and in defence against parasites. IgD has a role on B cells.

Vaccines train adaptive immunity safely by presenting an antigen without causing the disease. They can be live attenuated, as with BCG and measles vaccines, or they can use inactivated organisms, proteins or messenger RNA. Live vaccines are generally avoided in people with severe immune deficiency. Herd immunity means enough people are protected for spread to fall, which also protects those who cannot be vaccinated.

sections.heading: When immunity causes harm
sections.text:
Hypersensitivity reactions are classified into four types:
Type I: IgE-mediated allergy, including anaphylaxis, which is an emergency.
Type II: antibodies against cells, as in haemolytic disease of the newborn.
Type III: immune complexes, as in lupus nephritis.
Type IV: delayed and mediated by T cells, as in the tuberculin skin test.

Autoimmune diseases occur when immunity attacks the body’s own tissue, as in type 1 diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis. Immunodeficiency can be primary and genetic, or secondary to HIV, malnutrition or medicines such as chemotherapy. Patients with weak immunity have frequent, severe or unusual infections.

keyPoints: Innate immunity is fast and non-specific; adaptive immunity is specific with memory.
CD4 cells coordinate, and CD8 cells kill infected cells.
IgM appears first; IgG crosses the placenta.
Vaccines create memory without causing the disease.
Anaphylaxis is a type I reaction and an emergency.
Malnutrition and HIV are major causes of secondary immunodeficiency.

en.title: General pathology
en.short: Cell injury, inflammation, repair, thrombosis and cancer: the common mechanisms of disease.

sections.heading: Cell injury and inflammation
sections.text:
Pathology studies the causes and mechanisms of disease. Injured cells may recover if damage is mild. Severe injury causes necrosis, which is uncontrolled death with inflammation. The pattern gives clues: coagulative necrosis occurs in most infarcts, liquefactive necrosis in the brain, and caseous necrosis in tuberculosis. Apoptosis is programmed cell death without inflammation.

Acute inflammation brings redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function. Blood vessels widen and leak, and neutrophils arrive first. Chronic inflammation involves macrophages and lymphocytes and may form granulomas, as in tuberculosis and schistosomiasis. Repair occurs through regeneration or scar formation. Excess scarring can damage organs, as in liver cirrhosis.

sections.heading: Thrombosis and infarction
sections.text: A thrombus is a clot formed inside a blood vessel. Virchow’s triad names the three factors: vessel wall injury, slow blood flow and increased clotting tendency. An embolus is material carried in the blood that blocks a distant vessel. A deep vein thrombus can travel to the lung as a pulmonary embolus. An infarct is tissue death caused by loss of blood supply.

sections.heading: Neoplasia
sections.text:
A neoplasm is an abnormal growth that continues without normal control. Benign tumours stay local. Malignant tumours invade and spread, which is called metastasis. Carcinomas arise from epithelium, and sarcomas arise from connective tissue. Grade describes how abnormal the cells look. Stage describes how far the tumour has spread, often using the TNM system.

Cancer develops through accumulated mutations in oncogenes, which drive growth, and in tumour suppressor genes, such as TP53, which normally restrain it.

Some cancer causes are especially relevant in Africa:
Human papillomavirus causes most cervical cancer.
Hepatitis B and aflatoxin contribute to liver cancer.
Schistosoma haematobium is linked to bladder cancer.
Epstein-Barr virus is linked to Burkitt lymphoma.
Human herpesvirus 8 causes Kaposi sarcoma.

keyPoints: Necrosis is uncontrolled and inflammatory; apoptosis is programmed.
Caseous necrosis is typical of tuberculosis.
Neutrophils lead acute inflammation; macrophages and lymphocytes lead chronic inflammation.
Virchow’s triad: vessel injury, slow flow, increased clotting tendency.
Grade is how abnormal cells look; stage is how far the tumour has spread.
Several infections cause cancer, including HPV and hepatitis B.

en.title: Medical microbiology
en.short: Bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites, laboratory diagnosis, infection control and resistance.

sections.heading: Groups of organisms
sections.text:
Bacteria are single cells without a nucleus. The Gram stain divides most of them into Gram-positive, with a thick cell wall, and Gram-negative, with an outer membrane. Important examples include Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Escherichia coli and Salmonella Typhi, which causes typhoid. Neisseria meningitidis causes epidemic meningitis across the African meningitis belt, which runs from Senegal to Ethiopia.

Viruses need host cells to multiply. Examples include hepatitis B virus, influenza, measles and Lassa virus, which occurs in West Africa.

Fungi include Candida, and Cryptococcus, an important cause of meningitis in advanced HIV disease.

Parasites include protozoa, such as Plasmodium, and worms, such as Ascaris and Schistosoma. Many parasites have a life cycle with a vector or an intermediate host, and breaking that cycle is the basis of prevention.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.text: Good results depend on good samples, so collect them correctly and, where possible, before antimicrobial treatment. Microscopy gives quick information. Culture grows the organism and allows sensitivity testing. Serology detects antibodies or antigens. Molecular tests, such as PCR, detect genetic material. Results must always be interpreted with the clinical picture, because some organisms live harmlessly on the body.

sections.heading: Treatment and resistance
sections.text:
Antimicrobials target features that differ from human cells. Beta-lactams, such as penicillins, block cell wall synthesis. Macrolides block bacterial ribosomes. Fluoroquinolones block DNA gyrase. Antibiotics do not work against viruses.

Antimicrobial resistance develops when organisms survive exposure and spread. Unnecessary use, unsuitable or inadequate treatment, poor-quality medicines and weak infection control all contribute. WHO treats it as a major global health threat. Antimicrobial stewardship means prescribing only when needed, with the right agent and the right duration, according to local guidance.

Infection prevention protects patients and staff. Its foundations are hand hygiene, clean water, sterilisation, safe injections and vaccination.

keyPoints: The Gram stain divides bacteria by their cell wall structure.
Collect samples, where possible, before starting antimicrobials.
Beta-lactams act on the cell wall, and macrolides on the ribosome.
Antibiotics do not treat viral infections.
Antimicrobial resistance is a major global threat.
Hand hygiene is a basic part of infection prevention.

en.title: Principles of pharmacology
en.short: How the body handles medicines, how medicines act, adverse reactions and safe prescribing concepts.

sections.heading: Pharmacokinetics
sections.text:
Pharmacokinetics describes what the body does to a medicine. It has four stages: absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion. Bioavailability is the fraction that reaches the circulation. First-pass metabolism reduces this when the liver or gut breaks down a medicine before it reaches the circulation.

The half-life is the time taken for the plasma concentration to fall by half. It helps explain how often a medicine is given and how long its effect lasts. The liver and kidneys are the main routes of elimination, so disease in these organs can cause a medicine to accumulate. Liver enzymes in the cytochrome P450 family cause many interactions. Rifampicin, for example, induces them and can reduce the effect of other medicines.

sections.heading: Pharmacodynamics
sections.text:
Pharmacodynamics describes what a medicine does to the body. Many medicines act on receptors. An agonist activates a receptor, and an antagonist blocks it. Others act on enzymes, ion channels or transporters. Examples of classes and targets:
Beta blockers block beta-adrenergic receptors.
ACE inhibitors block the formation of angiotensin II.
NSAIDs inhibit cyclo-oxygenase enzymes.
Proton pump inhibitors block acid secretion in the stomach.
Opioids activate opioid receptors.

The therapeutic index compares the amount that causes toxicity with the amount that produces the effect. A narrow index, as with lithium, warfarin and digoxin, means little margin for error.

sections.heading: Safety and rational use
sections.text:
Adverse reactions may be predictable from the mechanism, or they may be unexpected, such as severe allergy. Risk is greater in pregnancy, childhood, older age, and kidney or liver disease. Taking many medicines together, called polypharmacy, also raises risk.

Rational prescribing means the right medicine for the right person, based on evidence, cost and local availability. The WHO Model List of Essential Medicines helps countries to choose. Falsified and substandard medicines remain a real concern in many markets.

This summary teaches concepts and gives no doses. Clinicians use current national formularies, and doses change. Nobody should start, stop or change a medicine based on these notes.

keyPoints: Pharmacokinetics: absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion.
Half-life is the time for plasma concentration to halve.
Agonists activate receptors; antagonists block them.
A narrow therapeutic index leaves little margin for error.
Rifampicin induces liver enzymes and causes interactions.
Always use the current formulary, because guidance changes.

en.title: History taking and communication
en.short: The structure of a clinical history and how to listen, ask and explain with respect.

sections.heading: Why history matters
sections.text: The history usually provides more diagnostic information than any other step. It also builds the relationship between patient and clinician. Begin by greeting the person, introducing yourself, and confirming their identity and consent. Ensure privacy. Use a professional interpreter if there is a language barrier, because relatives may unintentionally change the meaning or the patient may not speak freely.

sections.heading: The structure
sections.text:
A standard history includes:
Presenting complaint, in the patient’s own words.
History of the presenting complaint.
Past medical and surgical history.
Drug history, including allergies, over-the-counter products and herbal or traditional remedies.
Family history, including inherited conditions such as sickle cell disease.
Social history, including work, housing, tobacco, alcohol, finances and access to care.
Review of other body systems.

For pain, many students use SOCRATES: site, onset, character, radiation, associated symptoms, timing, exacerbating and relieving factors, and severity.

Women of reproductive age should be asked about menstruation and possible pregnancy, because this may change the diagnosis and safe investigations. Children need a birth, feeding, growth, development and immunisation history.

sections.heading: How to ask
sections.text:
Start with open questions, such as “Tell me what brought you here today.” Then allow the person to speak without interruption. Move to closed questions to check specific details, and include important negatives, such as the absence of fever. Ask about the patient’s ideas, concerns and expectations, because these explain why the person came and what would help.

Ask sensitive questions about sexual health, mental health, violence or substance use calmly and without judgement. Explain why you are asking. Summarise what you heard and check that it is right.

Example: Fatima, aged 30, attends with a fever. Her travel, pregnancy status, sick contacts and any recent antimalarials all change what is likely. She also worries about the cost of tests. Both kinds of information matter to the plan.

keyPoints: The history usually gives the most diagnostic information.
Begin with open questions, then use closed questions.
Always ask about allergies and herbal or traditional remedies.
SOCRATES structures a history of pain.
Explore the patient’s ideas, concerns and expectations.
Use professional interpreters where possible.

en.title: Physical examination and clinical reasoning
en.short: Vital signs, general signs, including on darker skin, and how to reach a differential diagnosis.

sections.heading: Approach to examination
sections.text:
Explain what you will do and obtain consent. Offer a chaperone for intimate examinations. Wash your hands. Keep the patient covered as far as possible. The usual sequence is inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation, although many teachers listen to the abdomen before palpating it, and neurological examination has its own order.

Vital signs include temperature, pulse, blood pressure, breathing rate and oxygen saturation. Typical resting values for an adult are a pulse of 60 to 100 beats per minute and a breathing rate of 12 to 20 per minute. Children have different normal ranges according to age. A breathing rate that is abnormally fast is one of the most useful early signs of serious illness.

sections.heading: General signs and darker skin
sections.text:
Look for pallor, jaundice, cyanosis, finger clubbing, oedema and enlarged lymph nodes. Signs can look different across skin tones, and most textbook images show lighter skin. Check pallor in the conjunctivae, palms, nail beds and tongue. Check jaundice in the sclerae. Check central cyanosis in the tongue and lips. Rashes may appear darker or purple instead of red.

Pulse oximeters may overestimate oxygen saturation in people with darker skin, according to several studies. Interpret readings with the whole clinical picture.

sections.heading: Clinical reasoning
sections.text:
Reasoning moves from information to a working diagnosis. Summarise the case in one or two sentences. Then list a differential diagnosis, which is the range of conditions that could explain the findings. Rank them by likelihood, and always consider dangerous conditions that must not be missed.

Each test should answer a question. The chance of disease before the test affects what a result means. For example, a positive result in a low-risk person may be a false positive.

Common errors include premature closure, anchoring on a first impression and ignoring findings that do not fit. Reassess when the patient does not improve. Ask a senior colleague for help when uncertain. A doctor who asks early protects the patient.

keyPoints: Consent, hand hygiene and dignity come first.
The usual order is inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation.
On darker skin, check pallor in conjunctivae, palms and tongue.
Check jaundice in the sclerae.
List a differential diagnosis, including dangerous causes.
Reassess when the course does not fit the diagnosis.

en.title: Medical ethics and professionalism
en.short: The four principles, consent, capacity, confidentiality and the duties of a doctor.

sections.heading: Four principles
sections.text: A widely used framework names four principles. Autonomy respects a person’s right to make decisions about their own body. Beneficence means acting for the patient’s benefit. Non-maleficence means avoiding harm. Justice means treating people fairly and sharing limited resources fairly. The principles can conflict, and careful reasoning is then needed. Different cultures may also place more weight on family or community decision making, which good doctors explore with respect.

sections.heading: Consent and capacity
sections.text:
Valid consent needs three things. The person must have capacity, must have enough information about the options and their risks, and must decide voluntarily. Consent may be withdrawn. Capacity relates to a specific decision at a specific time. A person with a mental illness may still have capacity, and a person who makes an unusual decision is not necessarily lacking it.

The rules for children and young people differ between countries. In England and Wales, for example, the 1985 Gillick case established that a child under 16 with sufficient understanding may consent to some treatment. Do not assume that this rule applies elsewhere. Emergency care without consent is generally accepted when a person lacks capacity and treatment cannot wait, subject to local law.

sections.heading: Confidentiality and professional duties
sections.text:
Information about a patient is confidential and should not be shared without permission. Exceptions exist in law, such as notifiable diseases, some court orders and serious risk to others. Take special care with HIV status and genetic results, because disclosure can cause stigma and harm.

Professional bodies set standards. Examples are the Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria, the Medical and Dental Council of Ghana, the General Medical Council in the UK and the Health Professions Council of South Africa. Duties include honesty, keeping knowledge up to date, working within one’s competence and raising concerns about unsafe care.

Ethical problems also arise from limited resources, such as patients being unable to pay for treatment, and end-of-life decisions. Discuss these with senior colleagues and follow local law and policy.

keyPoints: The four principles are autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice.
Valid consent needs capacity, information and free choice.
Capacity is specific to a decision and a time.
Confidentiality has limited legal exceptions.
Laws on minors and consent differ between countries.
Doctors must work within their competence.

en.title: Malaria
en.short: The Plasmodium life cycle, severe disease, diagnosis, treatment classes and prevention.

sections.heading: Burden and life cycle
sections.text:
Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites. The bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito passes them to humans. WHO estimated about 282 million cases and 610,000 deaths worldwide in 2024. The WHO African Region had about 95% of these, and children under five accounted for about three-quarters of deaths in the region. P. falciparum is the deadliest species and the most common in Africa.

Sporozoites travel to the liver, multiply, and are released as merozoites that infect red cells. Red cell rupture causes the fever. P. vivax and P. ovale can stay dormant in the liver as hypnozoites and cause relapse.

sections.heading: Disease and diagnosis
sections.text:
Fever is the main symptom, with chills, headache and body pains. Symptoms are not specific, so a test is needed where possible. P. falciparum makes infected red cells stick to small vessels, which reduces blood flow to organs. Severe malaria can include impaired consciousness, seizures, severe anaemia, low blood glucose, acidosis, breathing difficulty and kidney injury. Young children, pregnant women, and people without immunity are especially at risk.

Diagnosis uses microscopy of thick and thin blood films, or rapid diagnostic tests. Gene deletions in some parasites can cause false negative results on some rapid tests.

sections.heading: Treatment and prevention concepts
sections.text:
WHO recommends artemisinin-based combination therapies for uncomplicated falciparum malaria. The artemisinin component rapidly reduces the parasite load, and a partner drug clears the rest. Severe malaria is a medical emergency treated in hospital, with injectable artesunate preferred. Partial artemisinin resistance has been confirmed in parts of East Africa, so guidance continues to change.

Prevention includes insecticide-treated nets, indoor spraying, preventive medicines in pregnancy and seasonal programmes for children in some areas. WHO recommends two vaccines for children in areas of moderate to high transmission: RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M.

This is teaching material and gives no doses. Anyone with a fever in a malaria area should seek prompt testing and care. Figures and guidelines change, so check WHO and national programme sources.

keyPoints: Female Anopheles mosquitoes transmit Plasmodium.
P. falciparum causes most severe malaria.
P. vivax and P. ovale can relapse from liver hypnozoites.
Confirm with microscopy or a rapid test where possible.
Artemisinin-based combinations are the WHO-recommended treatment class for falciparum malaria.
WHO recommends RTS,S and R21 vaccines for children in eligible areas.

en.title: HIV and AIDS
en.short: How HIV damages immunity, testing, opportunistic infections, antiretroviral classes and prevention.

sections.heading: The virus and its effects
sections.text:
Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is a retrovirus. It binds to the CD4 molecule and a co-receptor on immune cells. Reverse transcriptase copies its RNA into DNA, and integrase inserts that DNA into the host genome. CD4 cells gradually fall. Without treatment, this leads to advanced disease, known as acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), with opportunistic infections such as tuberculosis, cryptococcal meningitis and pneumocystis pneumonia, and cancers such as Kaposi sarcoma.

WHO estimated about 41 million people living with HIV at the end of 2025, about 64% of them in the African Region. HIV spreads through sexual contact, blood, and from mother to child during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding. It does not spread through casual contact, shared food or mosquito bites.

sections.heading: Testing and care
sections.text:
Rapid antibody tests give same-day results. A positive result needs confirmation under the national testing strategy. Tests may miss a very recent infection during the window period. Infants under 18 months need virological testing, because they carry maternal antibodies. Testing should be voluntary, confidential and accompanied by counselling.

WHO recommends antiretroviral therapy (ART) for everyone with HIV, whatever the CD4 count. ART combines drugs from different classes, usually an integrase inhibitor with nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors. ART does not cure HIV, but it allows a long and healthy life. People with an undetectable virus on ART do not pass HIV to sexual partners.

sections.heading: Prevention and dignity
sections.text:
Prevention combines condoms, testing, voluntary male circumcision in high-prevalence settings, harm reduction for people who inject drugs, and ART in pregnancy. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) protects HIV-negative people and is available as oral medicine, a vaginal ring and long-acting injections, depending on the setting. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is urgent and needs prompt clinical assessment.

Stigma stops people from testing and staying in care. Use respectful language and protect confidentiality. Treatment guidelines change often, so check WHO and national sources. These notes are not medical advice, and anyone with possible exposure should go to a local health service quickly.

keyPoints: HIV infects CD4 cells and integrates into the host genome.
WHO recommends ART for all people with HIV.
ART uses a combination of drug classes and does not cure HIV.
An undetectable virus on ART means no sexual transmission.
Infants under 18 months need virological tests.
Tuberculosis is the leading cause of death among people with HIV.

en.title: Tuberculosis
en.short: Transmission, latent and active TB, diagnosis, combination treatment, resistance and BCG.

sections.heading: Burden and pathology
sections.text:
Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, an acid-fast bacillus with a waxy cell wall. WHO estimated about 10.7 million people fell ill and 1.23 million died in 2024, making TB the leading single infectious cause of death. It spreads through the air when a person with lung TB coughs.

Inhaled bacilli are taken up by macrophages. Immune cells surround them and form granulomas with caseous necrosis. Many people then contain the infection without symptoms, which is called TB infection or latent TB. Active disease develops in a minority, often when immunity falls. HIV, diabetes, malnutrition, smoking and crowded living conditions all raise the risk. People with HIV are about 12 times more likely to develop TB disease.

sections.heading: Presentation and diagnosis
sections.text:
Lung TB typically causes a cough lasting more than two weeks, fever, night sweats, weight loss and sometimes coughing up blood. TB can also affect lymph nodes, the spine, the meninges and other sites.

WHO recommends rapid molecular tests as the initial diagnostic test, such as Xpert MTB/RIF, which also detects rifampicin resistance. Sputum microscopy and culture also have roles. Skin tests and blood interferon tests show infection but do not prove active disease.

sections.heading: Treatment and control
sections.text:
Drug-susceptible TB is treated with several drugs together for months, because single drugs select resistant organisms. Standard treatment uses isoniazid, which blocks mycolic acid synthesis, and rifampicin, which blocks bacterial RNA polymerase, with pyrazinamide and ethambutol. WHO describes treatment lasting 4 to 6 months depending on the regimen.

Multidrug-resistant TB resists at least isoniazid and rifampicin. It is treated with other regimens under specialist care. Stopping treatment early can cause relapse and resistance, so patient support is a central part of care.

BCG vaccine protects young children against severe forms, such as TB meningitis. Control depends on finding cases early, treating them fully, and preventing infection through ventilation and care of contacts.

A persistent cough needs local medical assessment. National programmes usually provide treatment, and guidelines change.

keyPoints: TB spreads through airborne droplets from the lungs.
Latent TB has no symptoms and is not infectious.
Cough for over two weeks, fever, night sweats and weight loss suggest TB.
Rapid molecular tests are WHO’s recommended first test.
Combination treatment prevents the selection of resistance.
BCG protects children against severe forms of TB.

en.title: Sickle cell disease
en.short: The genetics and mechanism of sickling, complications, diagnosis, care concepts and counselling.

sections.heading: Genetics and mechanism
sections.text:
Sickle cell disease is a group of inherited haemoglobin disorders. Valine replaces glutamic acid at position 6 of beta-globin, producing haemoglobin S (HbS). The most common severe form is HbSS, also called sickle cell anaemia. Other forms include HbSC and HbS combined with beta-thalassaemia. People with sickle cell trait (HbAS) carry one copy, are usually healthy, and have partial protection against severe falciparum malaria. This protection explains why the gene is common in malaria regions. Most affected babies are born in sub-Saharan Africa, and Nigeria has a particularly large number.

When deoxygenated, HbS polymerises and red cells become stiff and sickle-shaped. Haemolysis causes anaemia and jaundice. Vaso-occlusion blocks small vessels and causes pain and organ damage.

sections.heading: Complications and diagnosis
sections.text:
Acute problems include painful crises, acute chest syndrome, stroke, severe infection, splenic sequestration and aplastic crisis, often linked to parvovirus B19. The spleen is damaged early in life, so children are at high risk from encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae. Chronic problems include kidney disease, eye disease, avascular necrosis of the hip and leg ulcers. Fever, chest symptoms, severe pain or stroke signs need urgent medical care.

Diagnosis uses haemoglobin electrophoresis or high-performance liquid chromatography. A simple sickling test does not separate trait from disease. Newborn screening allows early protection and saves lives.

sections.heading: Care and counselling
sections.text:
Care aims to prevent complications and treat them promptly. Concepts include vaccination, antibiotic prophylaxis in early childhood, screening for stroke risk with transcranial Doppler, effective pain relief, and blood transfusion when indicated. Hydroxyurea, also called hydroxycarbamide, raises fetal haemoglobin and reduces crises. Stem cell transplantation can cure some patients. Gene therapies have been approved in some countries since 2023, but cost limits access.

WHO released its first guideline on sickle cell disease in pregnancy in 2025.

Counselling on genotype should be accurate and free of pressure or blame. Couples make their own decisions. Guidelines change, and these notes give no doses and are not medical advice.

keyPoints: A single amino acid change produces HbS.
Haemolysis and vaso-occlusion cause most features.
Sickle cell trait partly protects against severe falciparum malaria.
Early spleen damage raises the risk of serious infection.
A sickling test does not separate trait from disease.
Hydroxyurea raises fetal haemoglobin and reduces crises.

en.title: Hypertension and cardiovascular disease
en.short: Definitions, causes, organ damage, drug classes and prevention of heart disease and stroke.

sections.heading: Definition and causes
sections.text:
Hypertension is persistently raised arterial blood pressure. WHO uses a threshold of 140/90 mmHg or higher, measured on separate days. US guidelines (2017, updated in 2025) use 130/80 mmHg, so definitions differ between countries. WHO estimated that about 1.4 billion adults aged 30 to 79 had hypertension in 2024, and many did not know it. It usually has no symptoms, so routine measurement is necessary.

Primary (essential) hypertension has no single cause and accounts for most cases. Risk factors include age, family history, high salt intake, obesity, inactivity, alcohol and tobacco. Secondary causes include kidney disease, renal artery stenosis, endocrine disorders, some medicines and pre-eclampsia. Use the right cuff size, have the patient rest first and repeat measurements.

sections.heading: Organ damage and atherosclerosis
sections.text: Long-term high pressure damages the heart, brain, kidneys, eyes and blood vessels. It leads to left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, stroke, chronic kidney disease and retinopathy. It also speeds atherosclerosis, in which lipid-rich plaques form in arteries. A plaque can rupture and trigger a clot, which causes a heart attack or an ischaemic stroke. Risk is assessed across all factors, including diabetes, smoking and lipids.

sections.heading: Treatment concepts
sections.text:
Lifestyle measures include less salt, healthy weight, regular activity, no tobacco and limited alcohol. WHO names four main medicine classes:
ACE inhibitors block angiotensin II formation.
Angiotensin receptor blockers block its action.
Calcium channel blockers relax arterial muscle.
Thiazide-type diuretics reduce sodium and volume.

Many people need more than one class. The choice depends on age, other diseases, pregnancy status, cost and supply. NICE in the UK prefers a calcium channel blocker as a first option for adults of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin who do not have type 2 diabetes. ACE inhibitors and receptor blockers are avoided in pregnancy because they can harm the fetus.

Guidelines change and these notes give no doses. Very high readings with symptoms need urgent care. People should check their blood pressure at a local clinic and take decisions on treatment with a clinician.

keyPoints: WHO threshold: 140/90 mmHg or higher on separate days; other guidelines differ.
Most hypertension has no symptoms.
It is a major cause of stroke, heart failure and kidney disease.
Main classes: ACE inhibitors, receptor blockers, calcium channel blockers and thiazide-type diuretics.
ACE inhibitors and receptor blockers are avoided in pregnancy.
Reducing salt is an important lifestyle measure.

en.title: Diabetes mellitus
en.short: Types of diabetes, diagnostic values, acute and chronic complications, and treatment classes.

sections.heading: Types and mechanisms
sections.text:
Diabetes mellitus is long-term raised blood glucose caused by too little insulin, poor response to insulin, or both. WHO reported about 830 million people with diabetes in 2022, with a faster rise in low- and middle-income countries.

Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, so insulin is essential. Type 2 diabetes, which is much more common, involves insulin resistance and gradual beta cell failure. It is linked to genes, obesity and inactivity. It is often found late because early symptoms can be mild. Gestational diabetes first appears during pregnancy and raises risks for mother and baby.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.text:
Typical symptoms are thirst, frequent urination, weight loss and fatigue. Commonly used WHO diagnostic values are:
Fasting plasma glucose of 7.0 mmol/L or more.
Glucose of 11.1 mmol/L or more two hours after a glucose drink.
HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or more. WHO accepted this test in 2011, given reliable laboratory methods.

Without symptoms, a repeat test is usually needed to confirm. HbA1c reflects glucose over about three months. It can mislead in sickle cell disease, recent blood loss, recent transfusion and some other red cell conditions. Criteria differ for pregnancy, and between organisations.

sections.heading: Complications and treatment concepts
sections.text:
Acute emergencies include diabetic ketoacidosis, hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state and severe hypoglycaemia. Long-term damage affects small vessels, causing retinopathy, kidney disease and neuropathy, and large vessels, causing heart attack and stroke. Foot ulcers can lead to amputation, so regular foot care is essential.

Treatment includes diet, activity, education and management of blood pressure and lipids. Medicine classes include:
Biguanides, such as metformin, which reduce liver glucose production.
Sulfonylureas, which stimulate insulin release and can cause hypoglycaemia.
SGLT2 inhibitors, which increase glucose loss in urine.
GLP-1 receptor agonists, which increase insulin release and reduce appetite.
Insulin, which replaces the missing hormone.

These notes give no doses and are not medical advice. Insulin must not be stopped without clinical guidance, and anyone with symptoms should attend a local clinic. Guidelines change.

keyPoints: Type 1 is autoimmune; type 2 involves resistance and beta cell failure.
WHO values: fasting 7.0 mmol/L, two-hour 11.1 mmol/L, HbA1c 48 mmol/mol.
HbA1c can mislead in sickle cell disease.
Complications affect small and large vessels.
Sulfonylureas and insulin can cause hypoglycaemia.
Foot care prevents ulcers and amputation.

en.title: Internal medicine: common conditions
en.short: Heart failure, stroke, chronic kidney disease, liver disease, airway disease and anaemia.

sections.heading: Heart and brain
sections.text:
Heart failure is failure of the heart to supply the body’s needs at normal filling pressures. It causes breathlessness, fatigue and leg swelling. Common causes in Africa include hypertension, cardiomyopathy and rheumatic heart disease, which follows untreated group A streptococcal throat infection. Ischaemic heart disease is common worldwide and increasing.

A stroke is a sudden focal loss of brain function due to blocked or burst blood vessels. Ischaemic stroke is more common overall, and haemorrhagic stroke is relatively more common in some African populations. Signs include sudden facial droop, arm weakness and speech difficulty. Brain imaging separates the types, because treatment differs. A heart attack and a stroke are time-critical emergencies, so a person with these signs needs emergency care immediately.

sections.heading: Kidney and liver
sections.text:
Chronic kidney disease is abnormal kidney structure or function lasting more than three months, often with an estimated GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m². Main causes include hypertension, diabetes and glomerular disease. It may also cause anaemia and bone disease.

Chronic hepatitis B and C, and alcohol, are main causes of cirrhosis, which is permanent liver scarring. Features include jaundice, ascites and bleeding varices. Liver cancer risk also rises. Hepatitis B vaccine, including a birth dose where recommended, is the main prevention.

sections.heading: Lungs and blood
sections.text:
Asthma is reversible airway narrowing with inflammation, while chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is largely irreversible. Tobacco is the main cause of COPD globally, but smoke from cooking fuel is also important in many low-income homes. Spirometry helps to separate these. Pneumonia remains common in adults, often caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae.

Anaemia is low haemoglobin. Its size classification guides the search for a cause. Microcytic anaemia often reflects iron deficiency, macrocytic anaemia often reflects B12 or folate deficiency, and normocytic anaemia has many causes. Hookworm, malaria, heavy menstrual bleeding and poor diet all commonly contribute.

These notes give general teaching only. Treatment follows current guidelines and individual assessment by a clinician.

keyPoints: Heart failure in Africa is often linked to hypertension, cardiomyopathy and rheumatic disease.
Stroke is an emergency; imaging separates ischaemic from haemorrhagic types.
Chronic kidney disease lasts more than three months.
Hepatitis B is a major preventable cause of cirrhosis and liver cancer.
Asthma is largely reversible; COPD is not.
Red cell size guides the search for the cause of anaemia.

en.title: Principles of surgery
en.short: Perioperative care, wound healing, shock, trauma assessment, burns and the acute abdomen.

sections.heading: Safe surgery
sections.text:
Surgery treats disease by operation, but its principles start well before the theatre. Preoperative assessment reviews the person’s fitness, medicines and allergies, and confirms consent. The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, introduced in 2008, has checks before anaesthesia, before incision and before the patient leaves the theatre. Its use reduces complications. Asepsis, careful tissue handling and control of bleeding also reduce harm.

Wounds heal through haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation and remodelling. Infection, poor blood supply, diabetes, malnutrition and smoking delay healing. Common postoperative problems include bleeding, wound infection, chest infection and deep vein thrombosis.

Many people worldwide lack access to safe surgery. The 2015 Lancet Commission on Global Surgery estimated this number at five billion.

sections.heading: Shock and trauma
sections.text:
Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion. Its main types are hypovolaemic, such as from bleeding or fluid loss; cardiogenic; distributive, such as in sepsis or anaphylaxis; and obstructive, such as in tension pneumothorax.

Trauma care uses a structured primary survey, known as ABCDE: airway with cervical spine protection, breathing, circulation with bleeding control, disability and exposure. Life-threatening problems are treated as they are found. Road traffic injuries are a leading cause of trauma in many African countries.

Burns are assessed by depth and body surface area. The rule of nines estimates surface area in adults, and children need a different chart. Severe burns cause large fluid losses.

sections.heading: The acute abdomen
sections.text:
The acute abdomen is sudden severe abdominal pain that may need urgent surgery. Causes include appendicitis, bowel obstruction, perforation, ectopic pregnancy and strangulated hernia. In some regions, typhoid can perforate the small intestine. Peritonitis produces a rigid abdomen and pain on movement. Obstruction causes pain, vomiting, distension and failure to pass stool or gas.

Every woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain should have a pregnancy test, because a ruptured ectopic pregnancy can be fatal. Sudden severe abdominal pain, or major injury, needs emergency assessment at a local hospital.

keyPoints: The WHO checklist has three stages and reduces complications.
The types of shock are hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, distributive and obstructive.
Trauma assessment follows ABCDE.
The rule of nines estimates burn area in adults.
Exclude ectopic pregnancy in women of reproductive age with abdominal pain.
Typhoid can perforate the small intestine.

en.title: Paediatrics and child health
en.short: Growth, development, newborn care, immunisation, malnutrition and the main childhood illnesses.

sections.heading: Growth and development
sections.text:
Children are not small adults. Their normal vital signs, body proportions, medicine handling and communication differ by age. Growth is tracked on charts, using weight, height and head circumference. A single measure tells less than the trend. Milestones cover gross motor, fine motor, language and social skills. For example, many babies smile socially at about six weeks, sit without support at about six to eight months and walk by about 12 to 18 months. Ranges are wide, and concerns need specialist review.

WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, followed by safe complementary foods with continued breastfeeding. National immunisation schedules differ, so students should learn their own country’s programme.

sections.heading: The newborn
sections.text: Nearly half of deaths under five occur in the first 28 days of life. The main causes in newborns are prematurity, complications around birth and infection. The Apgar score assesses a newborn at one and five minutes. Essential care includes warmth, early breastfeeding, cord hygiene and infection prevention. Severe jaundice can cause brain damage, so babies with early or deep jaundice need urgent assessment.

sections.heading: Common illness and malnutrition
sections.text:
The WHO and UNICEF approach called Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) helps health workers assess a sick child. General danger signs in a child aged 2 months up to 5 years are inability to drink or breastfeed, vomiting everything, convulsions, and lethargy or unconsciousness. A child with any of these needs urgent referral.

Pneumonia, diarrhoea and malaria remain leading causes of death after the newborn period. Fast breathing and chest indrawing suggest pneumonia. Diarrhoea causes dehydration and is managed with oral rehydration solution and zinc under programme guidance.

WHO criteria for severe acute malnutrition in children aged 6 to 59 months are weight-for-height below −3 standard deviations, a mid-upper arm circumference below 115 mm, or nutritional oedema, typically pitting oedema of both feet.

Doctors must also recognise child abuse and follow local protection law. Doses in children are specialised and are not covered here. Any unwell child should be seen by a local health worker.

keyPoints: Children’s normal values change with age.
Follow growth trends instead of single measurements.
WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for six months.
IMCI danger signs need urgent referral.
Pneumonia, diarrhoea and malaria remain major child killers.
Severe acute malnutrition: low weight-for-height, MUAC below 115 mm, or nutritional oedema.

en.title: Obstetrics: pregnancy and childbirth
en.short: Antenatal care, normal labour and the main causes of maternal death.

sections.heading: Antenatal care
sections.text:
A pregnancy normally lasts about 40 weeks from the first day of the last menstrual period. Naegele’s rule estimates the due date by adding nine months and seven days to that date.
Worked example: A last period on 1 January gives an estimated date of 8 October. Early ultrasound gives a more accurate date.

The 2016 WHO model recommends at least eight antenatal contacts. Care includes checking blood pressure and growth, testing for anaemia, HIV and syphilis, identifying blood group, and giving tetanus protection. In malaria areas, it includes nets and preventive treatment.

sections.heading: Labour
sections.text: Labour has three stages. The first runs from regular contractions with cervical change to full dilatation. The second runs from full dilatation to birth of the baby. The third ends with delivery of the placenta. Monitoring tools, such as the partograph and the WHO Labour Care Guide, help staff to notice slow progress and to give respectful care. Obstructed labour can cause uterine rupture and obstetric fistula, so safe access to caesarean section is vital.

sections.heading: Maternal emergencies
sections.text:
WHO estimated about 260,000 maternal deaths in 2023, with about 70% in sub-Saharan Africa. Most are preventable. The main causes are severe bleeding, infection, hypertensive disorders, delivery complications and unsafe abortion.

Guidelines issued in 2025 by WHO, FIGO and ICM diagnose postpartum haemorrhage within 24 hours of birth at measured blood loss of 300 mL or more with an abnormal sign such as low blood pressure or a fast pulse, or at 500 mL or more. Older definitions used 500 mL after vaginal birth, and some national guidelines and exams may still use them. Causes are uterine atony, trauma, retained tissue and clotting disorders. Uterotonic medicines, such as oxytocin, stimulate contraction of the uterus.

Pre-eclampsia is new hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria or organ involvement. Eclampsia adds seizures. WHO recommends magnesium sulfate to prevent and treat these seizures.

The three delays model explains many deaths: delay in deciding to seek care, in reaching care, and in receiving care after arrival. Severe headache, heavy bleeding, fits, fever or reduced fetal movements need urgent care at a local health facility. These notes give no doses or personal advice, and guidelines change.

keyPoints: WHO’s 2016 model recommends at least eight antenatal contacts.
Naegele’s rule: last period plus nine months and seven days.
Labour has three stages.
Main causes of maternal death include bleeding, infection and hypertension.
Magnesium sulfate prevents and treats eclamptic seizures.
The three delays: deciding, reaching and receiving care.

en.title: Gynaecology and reproductive health
en.short: The menstrual cycle, common gynaecological conditions, contraception, infertility and cervical cancer.

sections.heading: Cycle and common conditions
sections.text:
The menstrual cycle is often about 28 days but varies between people. In the follicular phase, FSH stimulates a follicle that produces oestrogen, and the endometrium thickens. An LH surge triggers ovulation. In the luteal phase, progesterone prepares the endometrium. Menstruation begins if pregnancy does not occur.

Abnormal bleeding has structural causes, such as fibroids and polyps, and non-structural causes, such as hormonal disorders and blood clotting problems. Uterine fibroids are benign muscle tumours and are particularly common in Black women. Bleeding and pain in early pregnancy can be caused by miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy. A ruptured ectopic pregnancy is an emergency. Abortion laws differ widely between countries. Whatever the law, unsafe abortion is a major cause of death, and doctors must provide lawful care for complications without judgement.

sections.heading: Contraception and fertility
sections.text:
Contraception supports people’s health and choice. Combined hormonal methods prevent ovulation. Progestogen methods thicken cervical mucus and, in some cases, prevent ovulation. Intrauterine devices and implants are long-acting and highly effective. Condoms also reduce sexually transmitted infections. Choice must be free from pressure.

Infertility is usually defined as no pregnancy after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse. Both partners should be assessed, because male factors are common. In many African settings, tubal damage after pelvic infection is an important cause. Infertility can bring heavy stigma, especially for women, so care must be sensitive.

sections.heading: Infection, cancer and protection
sections.text:
Sexually transmitted infections, including chlamydia and gonorrhoea, can be silent and can cause pelvic inflammatory disease.

Persistent high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) causes most cervical cancer. It is largely preventable through HPV vaccination and screening.

Female genital mutilation has no health benefit and causes lasting harm. It is recognised internationally as a human rights violation. Survivors of sexual violence need confidential, respectful and urgent care, including emergency contraception and HIV prevention where appropriate.

These notes are for learning and are not medical advice. Anyone with concerns should see a local health worker. Laws and guidelines differ by country.

keyPoints: An LH surge triggers ovulation.
Ruptured ectopic pregnancy is a surgical emergency.
Contraceptive counselling must respect free choice.
Assess both partners in infertility.
HPV causes most cervical cancer, and vaccination helps to prevent it.
Abortion laws differ between countries; care for complications is a duty.

en.title: Psychiatry and mental health
en.short: Mental state examination, common disorders, medicine classes, suicide risk and respectful care.

sections.heading: Assessment
sections.text:
Mental disorders are common medical conditions, not personal failings. Classification systems include ICD-11 and DSM-5-TR. Assessment joins the history with a mental state examination, which covers appearance and behaviour, speech, mood, thought, perception, cognition and insight. Physical causes must also be considered, including thyroid disease, infection, substance use and medicines.

The patient’s culture affects how distress is described and understood. Many people first consult religious or traditional healers. WHO’s Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP) supports non-specialist health workers where few psychiatrists are available.

sections.heading: Common conditions
sections.text:
Depression involves persistent low mood or loss of interest for at least two weeks, with changes in sleep, appetite, energy and concentration. Anxiety disorders involve excess fear and worry that disturb daily life. Bipolar disorder includes episodes of mania, with raised mood and reduced need for sleep, and usually episodes of depression. Schizophrenia features delusions, hallucinations, disorganised thinking and reduced motivation. Other important conditions include post-traumatic stress disorder, substance use disorders, dementia, and delirium, which is an acute medical emergency.

Treatment combines psychological, social and medical care. Cognitive behavioural therapy is one example. Medicine classes include selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, which increase serotonin signalling; antipsychotics, which mainly block dopamine D2 receptors; and mood stabilisers, such as lithium. Medicines should be started or stopped only with a clinician.

sections.heading: Suicide and crisis care
sections.text:
Clinicians should ask about thoughts of suicide directly and with compassion. Asking does not put the idea into a person’s mind. Risk is assessed by exploring thoughts, plans, past attempts, substance use, hopelessness, support and protective factors. Safety planning and reducing access to means are recognised parts of prevention. Suicide is preventable, and recovery is common with support.

Mental health laws differ between countries.

If you or someone you know is in crisis or unwell, go to the nearest hospital or health centre or contact local emergency services. Tell a trusted person and do not stay alone. These notes teach concepts and do not replace care.

keyPoints: Assessment combines history, mental state examination and physical causes.
Depression lasts at least two weeks and includes low mood or loss of interest.
Delirium is an acute medical emergency.
Antipsychotics mainly block dopamine D2 receptors.
Asking about suicide directly does not cause it.
Anyone in crisis should seek local medical help immediately.

en.title: Community health and public health
en.short: Primary health care, levels of prevention, immunisation, water and sanitation, and outbreak response.

sections.heading: Health in communities
sections.text:
Community medicine looks at the health of whole populations. Health depends on social determinants, such as income, education, housing, food, gender and access to care. Doctors therefore need to work with community health workers, leaders and other sectors.

Primary health care is first-contact care, close to where people live. The 1978 Declaration of Alma-Ata made it central to the goal of health for all, and the 2018 Declaration of Astana renewed this commitment. Countries organise it differently. Ghana’s Community-based Health Planning and Services (CHPS) programme is one example of care based in the community. Universal health coverage means that people receive the services they need without financial hardship.

sections.heading: Levels of prevention
sections.text:
Prevention has three classic levels:
Primary prevention stops disease from starting, for example through vaccination, nets and safe water.
Secondary prevention finds disease early, for example through cervical screening and blood pressure checks.
Tertiary prevention reduces harm from established disease, for example through stroke rehabilitation.

The WHO Expanded Programme on Immunization began in 1974 and is among the most effective programmes in public health. Clean water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) prevent cholera, typhoid and many diarrhoeal diseases.

sections.heading: Indicators and outbreaks
sections.text:
Health indicators compare populations and track progress. Examples are the infant mortality rate, the under-five mortality rate and the maternal mortality ratio, which is expressed per 100,000 live births.
