An outbreak is more cases than expected in a place and time. The usual response has these steps:
Confirm the diagnosis and that an outbreak exists.
Define a case and count cases.
Describe them by person, place and time.
Form and test a hypothesis on the source.
Apply control measures and communicate clearly.
Continue surveillance.

Cholera, measles, meningitis, Lassa fever and Ebola are examples that often require rapid notification to national authorities. One Health recognises the links between human, animal and environmental health. Neglected tropical diseases, such as schistosomiasis and onchocerciasis, affect the poorest communities and are controlled by combined programmes.

keyPoints: Primary health care is first-contact care close to the community.
Prevention can be primary, secondary or tertiary.
Social determinants strongly shape health.
Clean water and sanitation prevent many diarrhoeal diseases.
Maternal mortality ratio is expressed per 100,000 live births.
Outbreak response: confirm, define, describe, test, control and communicate.

en.title: Epidemiology
en.short: Incidence, prevalence, study designs, risk measures, test accuracy, bias and confounding.

sections.heading: Measuring disease
sections.text: Epidemiology is the study of how disease is distributed in populations, and of the factors that determine it. John Snow’s work on cholera in London in 1854 is a classic early example. Incidence counts new cases over a period in a population at risk. Prevalence counts all existing cases at a given time. Long-lasting incurable conditions may have a high prevalence even with a low incidence. Effective HIV treatment, for example, can raise prevalence because people live longer.

sections.heading: Study designs and risk
sections.text:
Observational designs include cross-sectional studies, which measure prevalence at one time; case-control studies, which compare past exposures in people with and without a disease; and cohort studies, which follow exposed and unexposed people forward. Randomised controlled trials test interventions.

Worked example: In a cohort, 30 of 1,000 exposed people and 20 of 2,000 unexposed people develop a disease. The risks are 3% and 1%. The relative risk is 3 ÷ 1 = 3. The risk difference is 2 percentage points. Case-control studies usually report an odds ratio, because they cannot directly measure risk.

sections.heading: Tests, bias and causation
sections.text:
Sensitivity is the proportion of people with a disease who test positive. Specificity is the proportion without the disease who test negative.
Worked example: Among 1,000 people, 100 have the disease. Of those, 90 test positive, so sensitivity is 90%. Of the 900 without disease, 810 test negative, so specificity is 90%. There are 90 true positives and 90 false positives. The positive predictive value is therefore 90 ÷ 180 = 50%. Predictive values change with prevalence.

Bias is a systematic error, such as selection bias or recall bias. A confounder is a third factor linked to both exposure and outcome. Randomisation, restriction, matching and statistical adjustment can deal with confounding. Association does not prove causation. The Bradford Hill considerations, such as strength, consistency, temporality and dose-response, help the reasoning. Temporality, in which the cause comes before the effect, is essential.

keyPoints: Incidence is new cases; prevalence is all existing cases.
Cohort studies follow exposure forward; case-control studies look back.
Relative risk = risk in exposed ÷ risk in unexposed.
Sensitivity concerns those with disease; specificity concerns those without it.
Predictive values depend on prevalence.
A confounder is linked to both exposure and outcome.

en.title: Evidence-based medicine
en.short: Asking clinical questions, appraising trials, reading effect sizes and using guidelines critically.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text:
Evidence-based medicine joins the best available research with clinical expertise and each patient’s values and circumstances. Research alone does not make the decision.

The process has five steps: ask a focused question, find the evidence, appraise it, apply it and evaluate the result. PICO frames the question as population, intervention, comparison and outcome. For example: in adults with hypertension in a rural clinic (population), does community health worker support (intervention), compared with usual care (comparison), improve blood pressure control (outcome)?

sections.heading: Judging the evidence
sections.text:
Well-conducted systematic reviews and randomised controlled trials usually provide the strongest evidence on treatment effects. A systematic review searches for all relevant studies using a stated method. A meta-analysis combines their results statistically. The GRADE approach rates the certainty of evidence and the strength of recommendations.

When appraising a trial, ask how participants were randomised, whether allocation was concealed, who was blinded, how many were lost to follow-up, and whether analysis was by intention to treat. Ask also whether the participants resemble your patients. Many trials have been conducted in high-income countries, so results may not apply everywhere.

sections.heading: Reading the numbers
sections.text:
Worked example: In a trial, 10% of the control group and 5% of the treatment group have a stroke.
Absolute risk reduction: 10% − 5% = 5%.
Relative risk reduction: 5% ÷ 10% = 50%.
Number needed to treat: 100 ÷ 5 = 20.
Twenty people need the treatment for one additional person to avoid a stroke, over the trial period.

Relative figures can sound more impressive than absolute figures, so report both. A confidence interval shows the range of values compatible with the data. A P value is not the probability that a treatment works, and statistical significance does not prove clinical importance.

Guidelines summarise evidence, but they age and may reflect the context of their authors. Check the date, the source and the funding. Practice changes as new evidence appears, so lifelong learning is part of the profession.

keyPoints: EBM combines research, clinical expertise and patient values.
PICO: population, intervention, comparison, outcome.
Systematic reviews and randomised trials are strongest for treatment effects.
Number needed to treat = 100 ÷ absolute risk reduction in percent.
Report absolute as well as relative effects.
Statistical significance does not prove clinical importance.

en.title: Research methods and research ethics
en.short: Planning a health study, sampling, analysis, qualitative methods, ethics approval and reporting.

sections.heading: Planning a study
sections.text:
Good research begins with a clear question that fills a real gap. A literature review shows what is known. The protocol then states the aims, design, population, measures, analysis plan and timeline. The design must fit the question: a survey for prevalence, a cohort study for risk, a randomised trial for treatment effect, and qualitative methods for experience and meaning.

Sampling decides who takes part. Random sampling gives each person a known chance of selection and supports generalisation. Convenience sampling is easier but is more open to bias. Sample size depends on the expected effect, variation, significance level and required power. Power is the chance of detecting a real effect of a stated size.

sections.heading: Data and analysis
sections.text:
Define every variable before data collection, and test questionnaires in a pilot study. Continuous data, such as blood pressure, are often summarised by a mean and standard deviation, or by a median when skewed. Categorical data are summarised as proportions. Common tests include the t-test for comparing two means and the chi-squared test for comparing proportions. Regression can adjust for several factors together.

Qualitative research uses interviews, focus groups and observation to explore why and how. Thematic analysis identifies patterns in the text.

sections.heading: Ethics and reporting
sections.text:
The World Medical Association’s Declaration of Helsinki, first adopted in 1964 and revised since, sets ethical principles for research on humans. Past abuses, such as the US Tuskegee syphilis study, show why they are needed. Requirements include independent ethics committee approval, informed and voluntary consent, confidentiality, fair selection of participants, and balancing risks against benefits. Extra protection is needed for children, pregnant women and people with limited power to refuse. National bodies oversee this, such as Nigeria’s National Health Research Ethics Committee.

Researchers should register trials in advance and report them fully, whatever the result. CONSORT guides trial reports, PRISMA guides systematic reviews, and STROBE guides observational studies. Plagiarism, invented data and undisclosed conflicts of interest are serious misconduct.

keyPoints: The design must fit the question.
Sample size depends on effect size, variation, significance level and power.
Use the mean for symmetrical data and the median for skewed data.
Qualitative methods explore why and how.
The Declaration of Helsinki guides research on humans.
Register trials and report all results.
